source.title: Test-Time Scaling Makes Overtraining Compute-Optimal
source.authors: N. Roberts; Sung-Dae Cho; Zhiqi Gao; Tzu-Heng Huang; Albert Wu; Gabriel Orlanski; Avi Trost; E. K. Buchanan; Aws Albarghouthi; Frederic Sala

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests scaling and compute-optimal allocation with a joint pretraining and repeated-sampling framework, rather than reproducing the original studies’ measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own downstream task NLL/pass@k scaling fits, forecasts, and comparisons of overtrained with Chinchilla-optimal checkpoints. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows. The reported relative-error values used to compare the two forecasting approaches are included because they assess extrapolation of the fitted scaling predictions.
record.test_reason: The study sits in a new setting: downstream pass@k with repeated sampling under joint train and inference budgets. Its fitted N,D(,k) laws on downstream task NLL and accuracy are extrapolated to held-out overtrained checkpoints, which bears on V6. Its k=1 Chinchilla fit is checked against Hoffmann's frontier, a weak, figure-only bearing on V3. Most other results concern inference-corrected optimal allocation, a different objective from V3's training-compute-only optimum.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that, when the repeated-sampling inference cost is counted, the optimal model is substantially smaller and more overtrained than Chinchilla prescribes. They find this consistent across NLL- and accuracy-based approaches and eight tasks, validated on overtrained checkpoints, and persisting after FT/SFT. The post-training recommendation is somewhat subdued but not back to Chinchilla. They defer validation at larger scales.
record.recipe_differences: The study combines Chinchilla-style loss scaling with pass@k or negative-log-pass@k modeling and jointly optimizes training and repeated-sampling inference budgets. It evaluates downstream tasks rather than reproducing the original pretraining-loss measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The optimal overtraining recommendation is more aggressive for Approach 2 than Approach 1, and is somewhat subdued after FT or SFT relative to base models.

fits_no_version.finding: When an inference budget with repeated sampling (k=Cinf/2N) is added, the optimal allocation shifts to much smaller, heavily overtrained models. Empirically, overtrained checkpoints beat Chinchilla-optimal ones on pass@k, before and after FT/SFT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-aware compute-optimal allocation (training plus test-time sampling) favours far more tokens per parameter than training-only laws.

fits_no_version.finding: The inference-aware optimum depends on the modeling approach: accuracy-based modeling recommends more overtraining than NLL-based. It is attenuated after post-training but does not return to Chinchilla.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The inference-aware optimal split depends on the modeled metric and on post-training stage.

record.problems: The tested checkpoints are small (5M to 901M parameters), and the authors defer validation at larger scales. The extrapolation setup says 21 overtrained checkpoints while its results text says 16. No uncertainty intervals are reported. Task-by-task table values are difficult to assign from the flattened text extraction.
record.rows_left_out: Task-specific pass@k values in Tables 1 and 2 were not entered separately because the flattened extraction makes their row-to-value assignments ambiguous; the paper’s explicit aggregate statements across all eight tasks (Table 1) and across the three post-training tasks (Table 2) are recorded in r5-r7.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus N, D or C is never reported; only downstream task NLL and pass@k are measured.
No extrapolation of pretraining loss to runs orders of magnitude larger. The validation is within the same compute range, in the overtrained regime.
No fitted exponents a and b for the k=1 optimum are reported. The fit is to downstream task NLL, not pretraining loss. The frontier is extrapolated to 1e25 FLOPs and not validated there.
There is no comparison of architecture shape.
No other modality is tested. T² is fit to FT/SFT checkpoints, but the quality of the power-law fit after post-training is not reported.
Only eight easy tasks with models under 1B parameters. Prediction from pretraining loss (as opposed to N and D) is not tested separately.
The study does not examine how parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method change the pretraining compute-optimal split or exponents, or whether curves bend.

missing.what: The k=1 Chinchilla fit on task NLL reproduces Hoffmann's compute-optimal frontier (70B overlay, 20 tokens/param). This is figure only.
Per-task fits of the scaling law on downstream NLL and accuracy across budgets; the authors say overtraining predictions are stable across inference budgets.
Under inference correction, the Chinchilla-optimal frontier improves non-monotonically in Ctrain, while T² improves monotonically.

record.verdict_notes: Models are 5M–901M parameters with up to 2.56e19 FLOPs; the forecasts to 1e25 are unvalidated. The extrapolation test varies tokens per parameter, not scale, so it is not V2 evidence. Most rows concern an inference-inclusive objective, which differs from V3, and were relinked to none. Checkpoint count is inconsistent (21 in setup, 16 in results). No uncertainty is reported. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, training tokens, or compute. Its loss measurements are downstream-task NLL or negative log pass@k.
The extrapolation test concerns downstream task performance for the reported overtrained checkpoints, not held-out pretraining loss or runs orders of magnitude larger than the study’s models.

The paper compares fixed-budget optimal allocations with Chinchilla and reports overtraining trends, but does not state fitted power exponents for optimal parameter and token counts or test their stability at frontier model scales.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study uses text language models and does not test other modalities, repeated-data training, or transfer as a generalization of the same power-law form.
The study tests downstream tasks and pass@k forecasts on its selected tasks and small base-model population, not general downstream performance across model families and scales.

The study compares two modeling approaches and base versus post-trained settings, but does not establish that published laws generally disagree, that scaling curves bend away from a power law, or how parameter-counting and data choices affect exponents.
